verdicts.result: math_fetch R1. J_F with recourse, constant W: closed form and derivative
verdicts.evidence: Re-derived from the two events: if the gap R <= s the read starts at arrival (stall x, no hold); if R > s it lands at s + r, so stall = (x - (R - s))^+ and hold = (R - s - x)^+. Swapping the integrals gives E[stall] = integral_s^{s+x} F and E[hold] = M(s + x); with M' = -S the slope is c[F(s+x) - F(s)] - lambda L S(s+x) = S(s)[c F(x|s) - lambda L (1 - F(x|s))]. The sign is right: the slope is positive exactly when the chance of an arrival within x exceeds q. Own simulation of the policy (/home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/design_unified_1126/agents/verify_math/vf_fetch.py, block r1): 750 cells (gamma, Lomax alpha 3.5, Weibull k 0.6, three atoms, capped tool entry, uniform; c and lambda L including 0; x from 1 ms to 1,000 s; 5 starts), 1.5 M gaps per law, z-scores with the exact standard error (E[cost^2] by quadrature): worst |z| 3.65, and 3.13, 2.03, 2.14 in three reruns with other seeds, no cell repeating. Atoms: J continuous, left and right slopes -0.05 / -0.35 at s = 2 and -0.35 / +0.40 at s = 6 = 9 - x; the formula gives the right slopes. Counter-case to 'p_inf = 0 is enough': Lomax alpha 0.8 (proper law, infinite mean): E[min((R - x)^+, cut)] = 45, 153, 426, 1,069 for cut = 1e3, 1e5, 1e7, 1e9, so the hold and J_F are infinite at every finite start. Not academic: the quantiles quoted for the trace (tool p90 16.8 s to p99 213 s; human 1,040 s to 29,366 s) give tail exponents 0.91 and 0.69, below 1; the replayed tool gaps (p90 8.1 s, p99 82 s) give 1.0.
verdicts.corrected_statement: Add 'the remaining gap has a finite mean' to the conditions (p_inf = 0 is not enough). With it: J_F(s) = c x - c M(s) + (c + lambda L) M(s + x) + kappa L/beta, J_F(arrival) = c x + kappa L/beta, J_F continuous, right derivative S(s)[(c + lambda L) F(x|s) - lambda L] wherever S(s) > 0 (two-sided where the law has no atom at s or s + x). Without a finite mean (a chance of never returning, or a tail heavier than 1/t) and with lambda > 0, J_F is infinite at every finite start unless the landed copy has a drop time; with a drop time theta the slope in s is unchanged for s + r < theta.

verdicts.result: math_fetch R2. J_F for a random queue wait independent of the gap
verdicts.evidence: Re-derived (B): conditioning on W = w gives c x_w^+ + lambda L (-x_w)^+ - c M(s) + (c + lambda L) M(s + x_w^+); on {R > s}, R > s + (r - W)^+ is the same event as R + W > s + r, which gives dJ/ds = S(s)[(c + lambda L) Phi(s) - lambda L]. Simulation (2 M samples, Weibull k = 3 gap, gamma waits, r = 4 s; vf_fetch.py block r2): formula against simulated cost worst |z| 1.74; best start 28.5 s where Phi = q; with P(W <= r) = 0.143 < q = 0.6 arrival is best and the best delay after arrival is 4.35 s = Q_W(q) - r. Hidden assumption found: case (C) uses the same law of W after the arrival as before it. If the wait is observed at arrival (the engine's estimate has a median error of 0.4 to 0.5 s), a read released at arrival lands exactly at admission, arrival costs c E(r - W)^+ only, and J(s) = J_B(s) - lambda L E[(W - r)^+] F(s). Example: W = 0 or 30 s (half each), gap near 25 s, r = 4, c = 1, lambda L = 0.25: (B) and (C) both start at 23.75 s (cost 5.06 against 5.25 at arrival); with W seen at arrival, arrival costs 2.00 and is the optimum, the early start costs about 3.2. The summary's 'nothing is read before arrival iff P(W <= r) < q' is false in the 'only if' direction: W = 0, r = 4, exponential gap of mean 200 s, q = 0.5 has P(W <= r) = 1 and F(x|s) = 0.0198 < q for all s.
verdicts.corrected_statement: (B) stands. If nothing about W is learned at arrival, dJ/ds = S(s)[(c + lambda L) Phi(s) - lambda L] and re-timing after arrival does not move the best start. If W is observed at arrival, dJ/ds = S(s)[(c + lambda L) Phi(s) - lambda L (1 + h(s) E[(W - r)^+])], h the hazard of the gap: start only when Phi(s) >= q (1 + h(s) E[(W - r)^+]). final_theorem_list: Theorem 1 (Fetch: the cost of a start time). A session's turn has ended; R is the remaining time until its next request, S(t) = P(R > t), F = 1 - S, and M(t) = E[(R - t)^+] is the mean overshoot beyond t. Its prefix of L tokens is on the SSD only. A read needs r seconds from release until its pages are usable; a turn whose prefix is resident waits W seconds for the GPU; r and W are known constants and x = r - W > 0 is the part of the read the queue does not hide. Policy 'start s': release the read at time s if the request has not arrived, otherwise at the arrival; the landed copy stays until the turn is admitted. A second of stall (turn due, read not landed) costs c >= 0, a second of holding the landed L tokens costs lambda L >= 0, and each read costs a fixed kappa L / beta. If E[R] is finite, the expected cost is J_F(s) = c x - c M(s) + (c + lambda L) M(s + x) + kappa L / beta, with J_F(arrival) = c x + kappa L / beta; J_F is continuous and its right derivative is S(s) [ (c + lambda L) F(x|s) - lambda L ], where F(x|s) = P(R <= s + x | R > s) is the chance that a read started at s stalls its turn. So J_F falls while F(x|s) < q and rises while F(x|s) > q, with q = lambda L / (c + lambda L): q is the stall risk the read accepts, not its complement. If E[R] is infinite (the session may never return, or the tail is heavier than 1/t) and lambda > 0, J_F is infinite at every finite start: a copy staged before arrival then needs a drop time (Theorem 3).

Theorem 2 (When the threshold rule is optimal). Setting of Theorem 1 with E[R] finite. Let tau be the first time at which F(x|s) >= q (tau is the arrival if this never happens). (a) A start just after which F(x|s) < q is never optimal. (b) 'Start at tau' is optimal if and only if the integral from tau to s of S(u) (F(x|u) - q) du is >= 0 for every s > tau, the arrival included. A single crossing of q from below is sufficient; it is not necessary. (c) If F(x|s) is continuous in s, the rule is optimal for every price q in (0, 1) if and only if F(x|s) never falls as s grows; this holds for every x exactly when the gap has a rising hazard (-ln S convex), and a chance of never returning rules it out.

Theorem 3 (Falling hazard; a read with a drop time). Setting of Theorem 1. (a) If F(x|s) never rises in s (true when the hazard of R never rises) and E[R] is finite, J_F has no minimum strictly between now and the arrival: read now if c E[min(R, x)] >= lambda L E[(R - x)^+], that is E[min(R, x)] / E[R] >= q, and otherwise wait for the arrival; with prices fixed, once reading now stops winning as the session ages it never wins again. (b) Any law, a chance of never returning allowed. Let the landed copy be dropped at time theta >= s + r if the session has not returned (a later return reads at arrival), and let K_io = kappa L / beta + lambda L r_m be the fixed cost of one read, r_m being the seconds the read holds its pages before landing. The expected gain over reading at arrival is G(s, theta) = c * integral_s^{s+x} [S(v) - S(theta)] dv - lambda L * [ integral_{s+x}^{theta} S(v) dv - W S(theta) ] - K_io S(theta). Its derivative in s is minus the derivative of Theorem 1; its derivative in theta is S(theta) [K_net h(theta) - lambda L], with h the hazard of R and K_net = c x + K_io - lambda L W. A read before arrival pays if and only if G(s, theta) > 0 for some s and theta.

Theorem 4 (Uncertain queue wait). Setting of Theorem 1 with W random and independent of R, r constant. Let Phi(s) = P(R + W <= s + r | R > s): given that the session is still away at s, the chance that its turn would be admitted before a read released now lands. (a) If nothing about W is learned when the request arrives, dJ/ds = S(s) [ (c + lambda L) Phi(s) - lambda L ]; if P(W <= r) < q nothing is read before arrival, and a read released after arrival is delayed so that it lands at the q-quantile of the admission time. (b) If W is observed at arrival, a read released then lands exactly at admission, and dJ/ds = S(s) [ (c + lambda L) Phi(s) - lambda L (1 + h(s) E[(W - r)^+]) ], h being the hazard of R: a read before arrival needs Phi(s) >= q (1 + h(s) E[(W - r)^+]). In both cases P(W <= r) < q is sufficient for 'no read before arrival' and not necessary.

Theorem 5 (After arrival: where the read lands). The turn has arrived; D is the time at which it would be admitted if its prefix were resident, with distribution function F_D as known now; the read time r is known; lateness costs c per second and earliness lambda L per second, both linear. The cost c E[(l - D)^+] + lambda L E[(D - l)^+] is convex in the landing time l and is smallest at l* = max(now + r, Q_D(q)), Q_D(q) being the q-quantile of D and q = lambda L / (c + lambda L); when the constraint does not bind, P(D <= l*) = q, so q is the chance that the turn is due before its read lands. If the read time is uncertain, the best release time is max(now, the q-quantile of D - r), whatever the dependence between D and r. For c = 0 every landing after the latest possible D costs the same, so the rule needs a floor on c. If a read cannot be re-timed once released and the estimate of D keeps changing, the first time at which P(D <= t + r | what is known at t) >= q is never later than the best release time, and is the best one if that probability then stays above q.

Theorem 6 (A read before arrival against a copy that never left). Symbols of Theorems 1 and 3; any law; drop time theta. Measured against 'no copy from age s on, read at arrival', keeping a copy from s to theta gains G_keep(s, theta) = integral_s^theta S(u) [K_net h(u) - lambda L] du, and G_keep(s, theta) - G(s, theta) = S(s) { (c + lambda L) E[(x - R_s)^+] + kappa L / beta - lambda L (r - r_m) } for every theta, R_s being the remaining gap of a session still away at s. Hence: (i) not evicting and reading back at the turn's end are not the same; they differ by this margin. (ii) If the margin is >= 0, which holds when a read is charged rent for its whole duration (r_m = r) or when kappa / beta >= lambda (r - r_m), a read before arrival pays only where keeping a copy would pay; with a hazard that never rises and unchanged prices, a copy that Retain dropped is then never worth reading back before arrival. (iii) If reads wait in the device's line without holding pages and device time is cheap, the margin can be negative and a read released before arrival can pay even on such a key. (iv) After a fall of the price or a forced eviction, a missing copy that Retain would keep is read back at once.

Theorem 7 (Retain: the holding index). A prefix of L tokens of an idle session is in host memory. G is the gap (G = infinity: the session never returns), S(t) = P(G > t), I(t) = integral_0^t S. At idle age a let F(h|a) = P(G <= a + h | G > a) and tau(h|a) = E[min(G - a, h) | G > a]. Holding costs lambda L per second; if the prefix is dropped before the return, the return pays K >= 0, where K depends neither on lambda nor on the drop age; the only information over time is that the session is not back; a dropped prefix is not read back before the return. Let nu(a) = (K / L) * sup over h > 0 of F(h|a) / tau(h|a). Then (i) dropping at age a is optimal if and only if nu(a) <= lambda, and keeping is strictly better if and only if nu(a) > lambda; (ii) the first age at which nu <= lambda is the earliest optimal drop age, and the same test is optimal at every later age however that age was reached; (iii) the set of ages at which dropping is optimal grows with lambda, so nu is the Gittins index of this stopping problem and the Whittle index of the session; (iv) (L/K) nu(a) is minus the slope of the first edge, from the point of age a, of the lower convex hull of the curve t -> (I(t), S(t)), t >= a, so the index at every age of an n-point law costs O(n).

Theorem 8 (Special cases of the index). Setting of Theorem 7, eta the hazard of G. Exact hint (return in R0 seconds): nu = K / (L R0), and K (1 - p) / (L R0) if with probability p the session has ended instead. Hazard never rising from age a on (a chance of never returning allowed): nu(a) = (K/L) eta(a+), falling with age; with one law for all sessions and equal K/L the eviction order is least recently used. Hazard never falling (this forces P(G = infinity) = 0): nu(a) = (K/L) / E[G - a | G > a], rising with age, and the priced decision is made once: keep to the return if and only if K >= lambda L E[G]. Sharp hint that may never be honoured (G = infinity with probability p, otherwise a law whose density does not fall on a support ending at b): nu(a) = (K/L) P(return | not back at a) / E[min(G, b) - a | G > a]. Ended session: nu = 0. Always nu(a) >= (K/L) eta(a+). Lognormal gap (ln G normal with standard deviation s): the hazard rises up to median * exp(s z*), z* solving phi(z) / (1 - Phi(z)) - z = s, and falls after; it is still rising at the median if and only if s < 0.798, i.e. p90/p50 < 2.78; past the peak nu(a) = (K/L) eta(a), and before it nu(a) = (K/L) eta(b), b being the point past the peak with eta(b) (I(b) - I(a)) = S(a) - S(b). A rule that keeps while (K/L) x hazard >= lambda therefore evicts every lognormal-hinted prefix at its turn's end; the index does not.

Theorem 9 (One index for idle prefixes, staged reads and queued turns). A clean prefix of L tokens is in host memory. Its session returns after a remaining gap R (R = 0 if the turn has arrived) and is admitted W seconds later, W independent of R with mean w. If the copy is dropped, the turn restores it at its arrival at a cost K0 that does not contain lambda (K0 = kappa L / beta + c E[(r - W)^+]), and the restored copy occupies L tokens for rho seconds before admission. Let g(a) = inf over h of tau(h|a) / F(h|a), the expected holding time per return over the best horizon: 0 for an arrived turn, R0 for an exact hint, 1/hazard past the hazard's peak, E[R] for a rising hazard, infinite for an ended session. Keeping (to some horizon, and through the queue once the turn arrives) beats dropping now if and only if lambda < nu(a) = (K0 / L) / (g(a) + w - rho), with nu infinite when g + w <= rho. For a queued turn nu = K0 / (L (W - rho)); for an idle prefix with no queue and a hazard eta past its peak nu = (K0/L) eta / (1 - rho eta). All host holders are ranked by this one number; staged reads do not yield before queued turns as a class.

Theorem 10 (Many sessions). Sessions i = 1..N with gaps independent across sessions given the hints, restore costs K_i and sizes L_i not affected by the policy, no read-back before the return. (a) Relaxed problem (held tokens <= C on time average): there is a price lambda* >= 0 such that 'every session drops its prefix at the first age its index reaches lambda*', with a coin flip between the two tie-breaking versions for at most one class of sessions, is optimal; lambda* = 0 if the unpriced demand fits. (b) For every lambda >= 0, sum_i v_i(lambda) - lambda C, v_i being session i's optimal priced cost rate, is a lower bound on the restore cost of every policy that respects C at every instant and has the same information. (c) Under the hard capacity, 'evict the lowest index when full' is exactly optimal for exact hints with equal sizes and equal costs (Belady's rule) and is not optimal in general: with one slot, A (cost 1, back in 10 s) and B (cost 1.05, back in 11 s), the index evicts B and pays 1.05 where evicting A pays 1. How close it comes to the bound of (b) is an empirical matter: in an equal-size simulation with the trace's two gap entries and room for a quarter of the sessions it is 28 % above the bound at 32 sessions, 3.5 % at 128 and within 1 % at 512, while LRU stays 29 to 34 % above.

Theorem 11 (The write: two lives of a dirty page). One idle gap, constant prices, a write that is instantaneous and costs w, no forced eviction. A page whose only copy below the GPU is in host memory (dirty) costs K_d at the return if it was dropped; a page with a complete SSD copy (clean) costs K_c <= K_d. With S, I and p_inf = P(G = infinity) as in Theorem 7: (a) writing strictly before the page is dropped is never better than writing at the moment it is dropped; for any horizon h within the clean page's holding time, 'hold h, then write if the session is not back' costs exactly w F(h|a) less than 'write now'. (b) The optimal life is one of two: hold until the first age at which the index with restore cost K_c + w falls to lambda, then write and drop; or hold until the first age at which the index with restore cost K_d falls to lambda, then drop unwritten. The first is chosen if and only if V0(K_d) - V0(K_c + w) >= w p_inf, where V0(K) = min over s of [lambda L I(s) + K (S(s) - p_inf)]. (c) V0(K_d) - V0(K_c) equals the integral over K from K_c to K_d of the probability that a page of restore cost K, under its own optimal rule, is dropped before a return. (d) A page of an ended session is never written. Over several gaps (the page stays dirty across returns until it is written), (a) still holds and the test of (b) is sufficient for writing but not necessary, because a write also serves the later gaps.

Theorem 12 (Due date of a write and order of writes). Setting of Theorem 11. Let d_w be the first idle age at which the page's clean index falls to lambda. Holding the page beyond d_w only because it is dirty costs, per second and given that the session is not back, L (lambda - (K_c / L) eta(age)), which is 0 at d_w and tends to lambda L only as the hazard dies: the due date is soft, and 'lambda L per second late' is an upper bound. For writes of equal size whose lateness is charged by one convex non-decreasing function, serving in every slot the released write with the earliest due date minimises the total lateness cost; with a concave shape or page-specific shapes it does not. When every waiting write is overdue with constant cost rates L_j (lambda - nu_j), the optimal order is lowest clean index first, whatever the sizes.

Theorem 13 (Order on the device). One device; transfer j (a read or a write) has a release time, a size p_j in device-seconds and a due date d_j; C_j is its completion time. (a) With all transfers released, serving in order of due date minimises the maximum lateness max_j (C_j - d_j). (b) With release times and preemption at any instant, always serving the released transfer with the earliest due date minimises the maximum lateness, whose optimum is L* = max over pairs (r, d) of [r + (work of the transfers released at or after r and due by d) - d]; hence if any schedule meets every due date, this one does. (c) If transfers can be interrupted only between pieces of at most p_max device-seconds, the same rule has maximum lateness below L* + p_max and need not be optimal. (d) A write that must finish before a given read can start is handled by giving the write the due date min(its own, the read's due date minus the read's size). (e) These are statements about the maximum lateness. For the weighted sum of lateness, sum_j w_j (C_j - d_j)^+, earliest due date is optimal when it meets every due date, largest w_j / p_j first is optimal when every waiting transfer is already late, and in between neither is optimal and the problem is NP-hard.

Theorem 14 (Read or recompute). A turn arrives whose prefix of L tokens is not in memory. If it is read back, the pages are usable V + lags + L / beta seconds after arrival (V the wait in the device's line, beta the device rate in tokens per second); the turn would get the GPU W seconds after arrival; a second of stall costs c and a device-second kappa. If it is recomputed, it takes gamma GPU-seconds per token, each costing mu seconds of summed TTFT (mu counts the turn itself). With lambda = 0, read if and only if mu gamma L > c (V + lags + L / beta - W)^+ + kappa L / beta. With D0 = V + lags - W: if D0 >= 0, read if and only if mu gamma > (c + kappa) / beta and L > c D0 / (mu gamma - (c + kappa) / beta). If D0 < 0: read at every length when mu gamma >= (c + kappa) / beta; recompute at every length when mu gamma <= kappa / beta; otherwise read if and only if L < c (-D0) / ((c + kappa) / beta - mu gamma). With the constants measured on FA3 (gamma beta = 0.79 to 0.94, lags 0.9 s, V = W = 0, kappa = 0, c = 1): recompute at every length at mu = 1; read above 22 to 33 K tokens at mu = 2 and above 5.2 to 6.5 K at mu = 5.

Theorem 15 (Queue weights in an open first-come-first-served queue). One server, fixed arrival times, turn j needs s_j seconds of GPU. (a) Every wait is a convex, non-decreasing, piecewise-linear function of the work added to an earlier turn. Almost surely the summed wait has slope B_k in the work of turn k, B_k being the number of turns served after k in its busy period, and sum_k (1 + B_k) x (extra prefill of turn k) is a lower bound on the rise of summed TTFT for any amounts of extra work. (b) With Poisson arrivals of rate alpha and load rho < 1, E[B_k | Q turns waiting, x seconds of the current service left] = (Q + alpha x) / (1 - rho): a GPU-second costs 1 + (Q + alpha x) / (1 - rho) seconds of summed TTFT, not 1 + Q. (c) Pass-over. If a turn that is due is not ready for S seconds and ready turns are served meanwhile without the server idling, the summed wait changes by (the summed work of the turns that went ahead) - (their number) x (the stalled turn's work), which is zero for equal work. If no turn is ready, each idle second costs 1 + B. For short stalls in the M/G/1 queue the expected cost of a stall-second is 1 / E[exp(-alpha s)] (1 + rho for exponential work, exp(rho) for equal work), which is at least 1; so 'the chance that no other turn is ready' is not the weight of a stall-second there.

Theorem 16 (Closed loop). N users stay in session; each alternates a pause and one request. Over a window with completion rate X, mean time in the system R and Z = (time-average number of pausing users) / X, N / X = R + Z whatever the server. (a) One server that is never idle: adding delta to the work of the request in service, with delta small enough not to change the order of service, delays exactly one request of every user, so summed response time rises by N delta. (b) Pool-bound batch server (at most B turns run; prefill is serial and pauses decoding; a decode step with n running turns takes tau(n) and gives each a token): while the pool is always full of ready turns, 1 / X = P + tau(B) n_out / B (P prefill seconds and n_out output tokens per request) and mean TTFT = (N - B) / X - Z + t_pre (t_pre = admission to first token). One more second of prefill raises summed response time by N and summed TTFT by N minus the number of turns decoding at that moment. (c) Hence two policies under which the pool stays full, the prefill seconds per request are equal and the same requests complete have the same mean TTFT, whatever their read timing and device order; and mean TTFT >= (N - B) g0 - Z + p0 for every policy that keeps the system saturated, g0 being the GPU time per request with nothing recomputed and a full pool and p0 the prefill of a request's own new tokens. (d) With requests of unequal work no bound of the form base + mu x work holds for finite amounts in a closed loop: in a three-user example 0.2 s more work lowers summed response time by 8.4 s.

Theorem 17 (Preempt: who yields room). A read needs m tokens; holder j has L_j tokens and displacing it raises its priced cost by C_j >= 0; costs add up across holders at fixed prices. (a) If holders can be displaced in part at proportional cost, taking them in increasing C_j / L_j is optimal. (b) Taking whole holders in that order until m is covered costs less than the optimum plus the cost of the last holder taken and frees less than that holder's size beyond m; its ratio to the optimum is unbounded. (c) Walking the same order, recording the set 'holders taken so far plus this one' whenever a holder would complete the cover and skipping that holder, and returning the cheapest recorded set, costs at most twice the optimum.

Theorem 18 (The price of room, and a bound). (a) Filling the room C_H in decreasing index solves 'maximise sum_j nu_j L_j x_j subject to sum_j L_j x_j <= C_H, 0 <= x_j <= 1', and the multiplier of the room constraint is the index of the holder at which the room runs out, 0 if everything fits. (b) In the relaxed problem of Theorem 10 the price lambda* is the index of the marginal holders and lambda* x (demand - capacity) = 0. (c) Open model: arrivals, queue waits and the weights c and mu are not affected by the policy; sessions are independent given the hints; every held token is charged to one session; the per-session problems are solved with no device line. Then for any prices lambda, kappa, sigma >= 0 over a horizon T, the sum of the sessions' optimal priced costs minus (lambda C_H + kappa + sigma C_S) T is a lower bound on E sum over requests of [c x stall + mu gamma x recomputed tokens] for every policy that meets the host, device and SSD capacities with the same hints. It is not a bound in the closed loop (Theorem 16 d).

Theorem 19 (Stability of the write path, minimal model). Let d(t) be the dirty tokens in host memory; a share p(d) of reads, non-decreasing in d, is refused for lack of clean room and recomputed; a request then takes g0 + gamma L p GPU-seconds and the saturated loop completes 1 / (g0 + gamma L p) requests per second; each request creates D_w new tokens to write; writes drain at w tokens per second. Without further rules d' = (D_w + L p(d)) / (g0 + gamma L p(d)) - w, and when g0 > gamma D_w the inflow rises with d: for D_w / g0 < w < (D_w + L p_max) / (g0 + gamma L p_max) there are two stable states, d = 0 and the room's limit, separated by the tipping point at which p = (w g0 - D_w) / (L (1 - w gamma)). If a recomputed page that the SSD already holds complete is not written again, or if a read that finds no room waits instead of being refused, the inflow is at most D_w / g0 and d stays bounded by the burstiness of new tokens whenever the rate guaranteed to writes exceeds D_w / g0. Either rule alone is enough in this model.

Theorem 20 (SSD capacity with chained pages). A lookup starts just below the session's deepest resident page and reads stored pages down the chain until the first missing one. (a) For lookups that start above the pages concerned, deleting a later page of a chain instead of an earlier one never retrieves less; among all ways to delete m pages of a chain read from its root, deleting the last m is the unique optimum. (b) For a tree of page groups read from the root, with rho(v) the summed lookup rate of the sessions whose chain passes through group v and theta the value per token read instead of recomputed, the optimal stored set at an SSD price sigma per token-second is {v : theta rho(v) > sigma}; these sets are nested in sigma, a tail never outranks its head, and an ended session contributes nothing. (c) If a shared head is resident on some lookups, its SSD copy is worth theta x the sum over sessions of (rate of lookups that find the head not resident) x (head length + the session's stored chain below it); it is worth nothing if the head is always resident, and (a) then fails for it.

Theorem 21 (Backup from GPU to host). A page is on the GPU until the GPU gives it up at time d_G; every use of the page before d_G is served by the GPU copy. If making the host copy later costs nothing else (the copy does not delay the scheduler), then for lambda > 0 the best time for the copy is the latest feasible one, d_G minus the copy time: an earlier copy only pays rent. An existing mirror copy has index (cost of making the copy at d_G instead) / (L x (d_G - now - copy time)): 0 when the late copy is free, and (mu x copy time) / (time to GPU eviction) per token when the late copy blocks the scheduler, in which case the early copy is optimal whenever lambda x (time to GPU eviction) < mu / (copy rate).

Proposition 22 (Share of writes ever needed). If after each turn a session ends with probability e, and otherwise the following gap outlasts the host stay of its pages with probability x, independently from gap to gap, then a page is given up by the host while its session is alive with probability q = (1 - e) x / (x + e - x e). With e = 1/29.2 and x = 0.046 to 0.103 (a host stay of 30 to 60 s) q = 0.56 to 0.74, so a write deferred to its due date would skip a share 1 - q of the write volume. At a constant device price and with no forced eviction deferring is weakly optimal (Theorem 11 a); writing at once is optimal whenever the device is idle.

A finite mean gap is a real condition, not a formality. J_F with a copy held to admission is infinite not only when a session may never return but for any tail heavier than 1/t. The quantiles quoted for the trace give tail exponents of 0.91 (tool, p90 16.8 s to p99 213 s) and 0.69 (human, 1,040 s to 29,366 s), and the replayed tool gaps give 1.0. So in the replay the 1,200 s cap, not the hint, decides the rent of every staged read; the drop time of Theorem 3 belongs in the Fetch rule itself.

'Fetch before arrival is empty on falling-hazard keys' needs the read to pay rent for its whole duration or a priced device. When reads wait in the device's line without holding pages (pages are allocated at dispatch) and kappa is near 0, the margin of the Fetch-against-keep identity is negative and releasing a read early, to join the line, pays even though Retain drops the copy (my counterexample gains +2.0 s where keeping gains -0.57 s). This is the regime of campaign 34's read line (planned read time 8.3 s against 30 to 52 s actual). None of the three connected the identity to that regime.

The landing rule and the pass-over result contradict each other unless c is allowed to depend on the length of the stall. math_fetch R6 minimises a cost linear in lateness with a constant c; math_order_price 3 shows the mean cost of lateness is zero while ready turns keep the slot filled and about one second per second after that. The cost is therefore convex in lateness, the fixed-quantile rule is exact only for the linear model, and for the mean the due date of a read is the time at which the GPU would run out of ready turns, not D. No theorem in the three reports states the landing optimum under that cost.

Shared pages in host memory have no index in the draft or in the reports. Theorem 7 is per session, but 17 % of prompt tokens are held by earlier sessions and first requests find 24 %. A shared head is needed at the first return of any sharer and stays needed afterwards, so its holding problem is not a single stopping problem: for hazards past their peaks its myopic index is (K/L) times the sum of the sharers' hazards, each at its own idle age, and that sum jumps up whenever a sharer returns. math_retain R16 treats only the SSD copy of a shared head; math_order_price 7 only excludes shared pages from the bound.

With several gaps the structure survives (write only at the moment of dropping) but the test under-writes: in 39 of 300 random cases the several-gap optimum writes where the single-gap test says 'drop unwritten', never the reverse. From the pool-bound batch model, an empty slot costs about one second of the waiting turn plus N a / (B tau(B)) = 0.96 s of lost throughput per second, i.e. about 2 TTFT-seconds per slot-second, or about 6e-5 per token-second for a slot of 33 K tokens: some 50 times the host prices the reports infer (around 1e-6).
